aum.title: Total assets under management
aum.content:
AUM is the market value of client assets Franklin Templeton manages across its multi-affiliate platform (Franklin, Templeton, ClearBridge, Western Asset, Putnam, Royce, Clarion Partners, Benefit Street Partners, Lexington Partners and others). It moves with both net client flows and market performance, and it is the base the firm's fee revenue is levered to.

For Franklin Templeton: AUM hit a record ~$1.795tn at FY2026 year-end (~71% sold in the US), rebuilt largely by market appreciation and acquired scale (Putnam, Lexington, Benefit Street Partners) after years of net outflows in legacy active mutual funds.

What to watch:

  • How much of the YoY change is flows versus market appreciation (compare with Average AUM and net flows)
  • Whether growth is concentrated in lower-fee passive/cash products or higher-fee alternatives

aumMix.title: AUM by asset class
aumMix.content:
AUM split across the five product lines Franklin Templeton reports: equity, fixed income, alternative (private credit, real estate, PE secondaries via Benefit Street Partners, Clarion Partners, Lexington Partners), multi-asset, and cash management.

For Franklin Templeton: alternatives and equity carry materially higher fee rates than cash management or passive fixed income, so the mix matters more than the AUM total -- it is the firm's stated offset to structural fee compression in traditional active mutual funds.

What to watch:

  • Alternative AUM's share of the total rising (margin-accretive) versus cash management's share rising (margin-dilutive)
  • Fixed income AUM, the largest single bucket, against rate-driven flow swings

netFlows.title: Long-term net flows
netFlows.content:
Long-term inflows/outflows are new client money into (out of) fee-generating long-term products, excluding cash management sweep balances; net flows is the difference. Organic growth from flows is read separately from market-driven AUM appreciation.

For Franklin Templeton: the firm has run net outflows in its legacy active mutual fund franchise for most of the past decade; a swing to sustained positive long-term net flows (helped by ETFs, SMAs/Canvas and alternatives) would be the clearest sign the fee-compression story has turned.

What to watch:

  • Net flows turning positive and staying there across quarters, not one good one
  • Which asset class is driving inflows versus outflows (see the AUM mix chart)

feeRate.title: Effective fee rate
feeRate.content:
Investment management fee revenue as a percentage of average AUM, in basis points (1bp = 0.01%). It is the price Franklin Templeton realises on the assets it manages, before sales/distribution and servicing fees.

For Franklin Templeton: management reported the ex-performance-fee rate at roughly 40.7bps in FY2026, up slightly from 40.5bps in FY2025 -- a small reversal after years of gradual compression as cheaper passive and fixed income products grew faster than higher-fee active equity and alternatives.

What to watch:

  • Fee rate stabilising or compounding further: a few bps moves hundreds of millions of revenue on a ~$1.8tn base
  • Fee rate trend against the AUM mix chart -- a rate drop that tracks a shift toward cash management is structural, not cyclical

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.): the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
